reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Presents as symmetrical, poorly defined brown to grey-brown patches on sun-exposed facial skin, typically the cheeks, forehead, upper lip, and chin
It is far more common in women and in people with darker skin phototypes, and often follows pregnancy or hormonal exposure
Recognised patterns are centrofacial, malar, and mandibular; a similar eruption can also occur on the forearms
Wood's lamp examination can help gauge the depth of pigment, with epidermal pigment enhanced and dermal pigment less so, which influences treatment expectations
Ultraviolet and visible light, including screen and heat exposure, are major drivers, so broad-spectrum photoprotection with a tinted (iron-oxide-containing) product is the cornerstone of care
Combination topical lightening agents and gentle chemical peels can help, but aggressive procedures risk post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, especially in darker skin
Review and, where feasible, stop contributory hormonal exposures such as combined oral contraception
Set realistic expectations: recurrence is common and lifelong sun protection and maintenance are usually needed
reference.pathophysiology: Melasma reflects an acquired disorder of localised hyperpigmentation in which functionally hyperactive melanocytes deposit excess melanin in the epidermis, dermis, or both. Ultraviolet and visible light, hormonal influences (pregnancy, oestrogen), and a genetic predisposition upregulate melanogenic signalling, while an altered dermal environment with solar elastosis, increased vascularity, and a disrupted basement membrane allows pigment to drop into the dermis. This basement-membrane damage helps explain the chronic, relapsing nature and the resistance of dermal pigment to topical therapy.
additionalDifferentials: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation following acne or dermatitis
Solar lentigines and other photo-induced pigmentation
Ochronosis (which can be exogenous, from overuse of hydroquinone)
Naevus of Ota or acquired dermal melanocytosis
additionalInvestigations: Primarily a clinical diagnosis supported by dermoscopy
Wood's lamp examination to help assess pigment depth
Skin biopsy only in atypical or treatment-resistant cases
Review of hormonal and drug history as part of assessment
redFlags: Asymmetric, irregular, or evolving pigmented lesions raising concern for melanoma rather than melasma
Rapidly darkening or nodular change within a pigmented area
Paradoxical darkening or blue-black discolouration suggesting exogenous ochronosis from prolonged skin-lightening use
reference.prognosis: Melasma is typically chronic and relapsing; pregnancy-related disease may fade after delivery, but many patients experience persistence or recurrence, and long-term photoprotection with maintenance therapy is usually required to sustain improvement.
pitfalls: Neglecting visible-light protection and relying only on conventional UV sunscreen
Provoking post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation with overly aggressive peels or lasers in darker skin
Causing exogenous ochronosis through prolonged, unsupervised use of skin-lightening agents
Promising a permanent cure rather than emphasising control and maintenance
management: Apply rigorous broad-spectrum photoprotection with a tinted iron-oxide-containing sunscreen shielding against both ultraviolet and visible light as the cornerstone
Prescribe topical lightening therapy with hydroquinone, or a triple combination of hydroquinone, a retinoid and a corticosteroid, with alternatives such as azelaic acid or cysteamine
Use oral tranexamic acid for resistant or extensive disease
Add gentle superficial chemical peels as an adjunct, avoiding aggressive procedures that risk post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation
Identify and remove hormonal triggers such as combined oral contraceptives where feasible
Use laser and energy devices cautiously, particularly in darker skin phototypes
Continue long-term maintenance therapy and sustained photoprotection given the chronic relapsing course
